## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## dataforseo
DataForSEO API tools: browse documentation (docs_index, docs_list_sections, docs_search) and make authenticated API requests (api_request). 
   Prefer OAuth Bearer tokens via HTTP transport (authorization server https://data.dataforseo.com). 
   DATAFORSEO_LOGIN and DATAFORSEO_PASSWORD remain an optional env fallback. 
   Documentation cache directory can be set at server startup with --docs-cache-dir <path> (24h TTL).

- stripe:explain-error: Explain Stripe error codes and provide solutions with code examples
- stripe:test-cards: Display Stripe test card numbers for various testing scenarios
- codemyspec:design: Architecture design, UI design system, and technology strategy. Use before writing code to plan how to build it.
- codemyspec:develop: Full-lifecycle development — context orchestration, LiveView orchestration, and interactive refactoring. Spawns subagents for multi-step workflows.
- codemyspec:implement: Autonomous implementation loop — start or stop requirements-driven development. The agent walks the requirement graph automatically.
- codemyspec:init: Project setup, authentication, and sync. Use when starting a new project, logging in, or refreshing stale state.
- codemyspec:next: Find and start the next requirement task in one gesture. Use after each completed task as your single onboarding instruction.
- codemyspec:product: Product management — guided story interview, review, and Three Amigos sessions. Use when defining what to build, refining requirements, reviewing story quality, or running an Example Mapping session on a story.
- codemyspec:qa: QA testing and issue management — full app QA, per-story QA, integration planning, issue triage, and fixes.
- codemyspec:sync: Sync project components and regenerate architecture views. Use after git pulls, before design sessions, or when views feel stale.
- stripe:connect-recommend: This skill should be used when the user asks about Stripe Connect configuration, charge patterns, dashboard access, or how to get started with Connect, is building a marketplace, platform, multi-vendor store, gig platform, or subscription platform, needs to pay out sellers, vendors, or providers, mentions split payments, revenue sharing, multi-party payments, or similar payment distribution concepts, provides a company URL or business description for a recommendation, builds SaaS that routes money between parties (e.g. POS, booking, invoicing — not operational SaaS without payment routing), asks about onboarding or KYC for merchants/sellers/vendors, mentions connected account dashboard or responsibility configurations, or asks about payment flows, white-label payments, or embedded payments.
- stripe:stripe-best-practices: Guides Stripe integration decisions — API selection (Checkout Sessions vs PaymentIntents), Connect platform setup (Accounts v2, controller properties), billing/subscriptions, Treasury financial accounts, integration surfaces (Checkout, Payment Element), migrating from deprecated Stripe APIs, and security best practices (API key management, restricted keys, webhooks, OAuth). Use when building, modifying, or reviewing any Stripe integration — including accepting payments, building marketplaces, integrating Stripe, processing payments, setting up subscriptions, creating connected accounts, or implementing secure key handling.
- stripe:stripe-directory: Use when the user wants to find businesses, software, service providers, or partners for a specific industry, workflow, pain point, capability, or job to be done. Also use when the agent needs to programmatically purchase or consume a service. Use Stripe Directory to build a short relevant shortlist, even if the user does not mention Stripe Directory explicitly.
- stripe:stripe-projects: Use when the user wants to provision infrastructure or third-party services using Stripe Projects. Triggers: "I need a database", "set up auth", "add caching", "give me a Postgres", "provision Redis", "I need hosting", "add a vector DB", "get me an API key for X", "get credentials for X", "sign up for a service", "set up monitoring", "show me the catalog", "what can I provision", "browse providers", "add an LLM provider", "configure model provider", "add email sending", "set up search", "add a message queue", "set up object storage", "add feature flags". Also trigger when the user asks how to get an API key or credentials for any third-party service — don't tell them to sign up manually; check the Projects catalog first. Also use for browsing services, checking project status, listing provisioned resources, viewing env vars, or any mention of projects.dev or adding/provisioning/connecting a cloud service.
- stripe:upgrade-stripe: Guide for upgrading Stripe API versions and SDKs
- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever any such runtime behavior would make an artifact more useful, before writing the page.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- workflow-authoring: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

content.text:
# devops_status

Whether the infrastructure this account is supposed to have actually exists.

Answers three separate questions, because conflating them is what made
"is devops setup done?" unanswerable:

- **missing** — a step whose resources are not there. This is what decides
  whether `devops_setup` is complete.
- **dangling** — a resource that exists and points at nothing, usually a DNS
  record left over from a destroyed server. Not a completion problem; it is
  cleanup, and it does not block the requirement.
- **unreachable** — a provider that could not be read. This is the absence of
  an answer, not a verdict. Do not treat it as "not done".

Read from the providers, not from a record file. Setup completion used to be
decided by grepping a markdown file for the words "verified" and "prod",
which an agent could satisfy by writing prose.

## Never sees past the one project it is connected to

`Resources.report/1` is deliberately account-wide — the cross-project
dangling checks need to see everything, and that is right for `/app/
resources`, a human looking at their own whole account. It is wrong for
this tool: a caller reaching it through the harness is scoped to one
project's work, and has no business learning what devops state, missing
steps, or dangling resources some *other* project in the same account
carries. Confirmed live, twice: first a project whose own devops was
still `:off` got back a different project's checklist entirely; then,
once devops was turned on, that *same* other project kept appearing in
full detail beside the real answer, because the underlying call was still
`Resources.report/1`. This uses `Resources.project_report/2` instead,
which never runs `deployable/1` or asks a provider for anything beyond
the one project it is given — there is no account-wide data left to leak,
on or off.

## Arguments

  none

## Example

```lua
local result, err = devops_status({})
if result == nil then return "failed: " .. err.message end
return result
```

content.text:
# run_devops_setup

Build the infrastructure that is missing, for the project this call is
connected to.

This provisions **real resources in real accounts** — servers, DNS records,
buckets, sending domains — and they cost money and change where mail and
traffic go. It is the same run the provisioning page's per-project button
performs.

No `project_id` parameter, on purpose. This used to take one, and
separately accepted omitting it entirely as a bulk "build every project
whose devops level is not off" mode — either shape let a caller name (or
fail to name) a *different* project than the one this call is actually
connected to, sometimes triggering real, costed provisioning on projects
nobody asked to touch. Found during an audit prompted by a real,
unrelated cross-project leak in `devops_status`. The only project this
tool can ever act on now is `Validators.devops_project/1`'s answer —
whichever project the connection itself identifies (the harness's own
`X-Project-ID` header, or the configured project for stdio) — the same
fix applied to every other devops tool.

The sequence is ordered and halts on the first failure, which is deliberate —
the ordering *is* the dependency model. A step that pauses is waiting on a
decision only a person can make (a credential that cannot be minted through
an API, an apex that is already serving a live site); read what it says
rather than retrying it.

Call `devops_status` first. If it reports a provider unreachable, the answer
is unknown rather than "not done", and running setup on that basis may build
things that already exist.

## This returns as soon as the run starts, not when it finishes

A real run can take minutes — deploy alone has measured ~167s — which is
longer than this tool's own transport waits for a reply. Calling and then
waiting for a definitive "complete" here will time out even when the run is
proceeding normally; call `devops_status` afterward to watch it converge
instead of retrying this call. Retrying while a run is still going does not
start a second one — the project is locked for the run's duration and the
retry is told a run is already in progress, rather than racing the first
run's writes against the same provider.

## Arguments

  none

## Example

```lua
local result, err = run_devops_setup({})
if result == nil then return "failed: " .. err.message end
return result
```

content.text:
# provision_account_server

Bring up (or adopt) one account-owned server: the box itself, its shared
registry container, and its shared database container — ready for any
project to link an environment onto afterward.

This is the account-level half of the hard line stories 989/990 drew:
server and box-wide container creation live here, never in a project's own
devops step (`run_provisioning_step`/`run_devops_setup`), which refuses to
reach `Hetzner.create_server` under any circumstance
(`Steps.server_creation_gate/3`). Once this tool has run, a project points
an environment at the result with `link_server` — this tool never touches a
project or an environment itself.

Idempotent both ways — a name the provider already has is adopted, not
duplicated (`Hetzner.ensure_server/3`), and a name this account has already
linked stays linked (`Server.link/2`'s own `on_conflict: :nothing`). Safe to
call again for a box whose registry or database came up short the first
time; both container checks start from "is this already true" before doing
anything.

## Not yet restricted by identity

Nothing today restricts *who* may call this the way `server_creation_gate`
restricts what a project-scoped step may do. A dedicated account-level
agent — with its own tool set excluding this from every project-scoped
caller structurally, not just by convention — was part of the original
design for this split and was cut from this round of work as unnecessary
scope. Until something like it exists, this tool is reachable the same way
every other devops tool is: by whatever session is connected, through code
mode. The refusal that actually matters — no project-scoped path reaches
create-server — holds regardless, enforced in `Steps.ex` itself rather than
by who is allowed to call this tool.

## Arguments

  name (string, required)

## Example

```lua
local result, err = provision_account_server({ name = "…" })
if result == nil then return "failed: " .. err.message end
return result
```

toolUseResult.text:
# provision_account_server

Bring up (or adopt) one account-owned server: the box itself, its shared
registry container, and its shared database container — ready for any
project to link an environment onto afterward.

This is the account-level half of the hard line stories 989/990 drew:
server and box-wide container creation live here, never in a project's own
devops step (`run_provisioning_step`/`run_devops_setup`), which refuses to
reach `Hetzner.create_server` under any circumstance
(`Steps.server_creation_gate/3`). Once this tool has run, a project points
an environment at the result with `link_server` — this tool never touches a
project or an environment itself.

Idempotent both ways — a name the provider already has is adopted, not
duplicated (`Hetzner.ensure_server/3`), and a name this account has already
linked stays linked (`Server.link/2`'s own `on_conflict: :nothing`). Safe to
call again for a box whose registry or database came up short the first
time; both container checks start from "is this already true" before doing
anything.

## Not yet restricted by identity

Nothing today restricts *who* may call this the way `server_creation_gate`
restricts what a project-scoped step may do. A dedicated account-level
agent — with its own tool set excluding this from every project-scoped
caller structurally, not just by convention — was part of the original
design for this split and was cut from this round of work as unnecessary
scope. Until something like it exists, this tool is reachable the same way
every other devops tool is: by whatever session is connected, through code
mode. The refusal that actually matters — no project-scoped path reaches
create-server — holds regardless, enforced in `Steps.ex` itself rather than
by who is allowed to call this tool.

## Arguments

  name (string, required)

## Example

```lua
local result, err = provision_account_server({ name = "…" })
if result == nil then return "failed: " .. err.message end
return result
```

.code_my_spec/campaigns/dev_story/synthesis.md:5:It was built through the CodeMySpec harness from a single prompt. John typed roughly 110 words on July 7, 2026 at 16:44 UTC. About 2.5 days of wall clock later the app was deployed to UAT with live Stripe, a real email provider, and an external tester's feedback batch already fixed. The initial commit on July 9 contained 1,404 files and 103,875 insertions: 21 stories across 3 personas, 143 BDD criteria (105 happy path, 38 failure path) backed by 115 BDD rules, and 262 tests including 5 Wallaby browser journeys. By the end of July 9 the suite stood at 331 tests. Along the way the harness spawned 172 subagents, ran 36 QA attempts across the 21 stories (all eventually passing), and filed 35 issues: 6 critical, 15 high, 9 medium, 5 low.
.code_my_spec/campaigns/dev_story/synthesis.md:25:The specs themselves had bugs, six distinct classes of them. Two stories specced opposite behavior for the same situation; a spec agent refused to paper over it: "worth a decision on which behavior is authoritative before implementation." Five files had wrong dollar math versus their own gherkin. A shared regex assumed integer job IDs while jobs use UUIDs, so story 846 read 0/5 against a fully correct implementation until the orchestrator fixed the test helper.
.code_my_spec/campaigns/dev_story/synthesis.md:47:Then the environment melted down again, differently. Assets started 404ing mid-QA, the login page 500ed, and arbitrary modules went "not available" on some requests but not others. The QA agent escalated correctly: "this reads as the running release having a partially-loaded/inconsistent code path, not something for me to route around." Root cause: two zombie phx.server processes squatting the port, serving stale partial builds while implementers recompiled underneath. The orchestrator's fix was a new discipline invented mid-run: serve QA from an immutable `mix release` copy, rebuilt after each fix batch, a pattern that held for the rest of the build. Cost of the outage: about 40 minutes, zero John involvement.
.code_my_spec/campaigns/dev_story/synthesis.md:67:July 9 was the shipping day: 16 commits total, the initial commit at 14:19 UTC and 15 more behind it. John's messages shifted to delegation and credentials. "Check @../devops/ and get us a uat deploy of this" produced a Kamal-on-Hetzner deployment in about 75 minutes, including three consecutive deploy failures, each self-diagnosed: the agent had wrongly stripped npm steps from the Dockerfile ("package.json existed all along", it admitted, "my earlier check was wrong"), then a missing health route, then `force_ssl` 301ing the health probe.
.code_my_spec/campaigns/dev_story/synthesis.md:75:The last act came after midnight. John: "Dude you need to get that form testable... you need to get that tested and recording with reqcassette." The resulting cassette-backed Stripe tests found a real security hole within 15 minutes: webhook signature verification had no timestamp tolerance, so a correctly signed payload from a year earlier was accepted. It had been live on UAT. The fix, plus a deploy regression the health check caught safely (a test-only dependency pin broke the production boot path; the old container kept serving), closed the build at 331 tests and 143 specs green, July 10, 01:25 UTC.

.code_my_spec/campaigns/dev_story/synthesis.md:5:It was built through the CodeMySpec harness from a single prompt. John typed roughly 110 words on July 7, 2026 at 16:44 UTC. About 2.5 days of wall clock later the app was deployed to UAT with live Stripe, a real email provider, and an external tester's feedback batch already fixed. The initial commit on July 9 contained 1,404 files and 103,875 insertions: 21 stories across 3 personas, 143 BDD criteria (105 happy path, 38 failure path) backed by 115 BDD rules, and 262 tests including 5 Wallaby browser journeys. By the end of July 9 the suite stood at 331 tests. Along the way the harness spawned 172 subagents, ran 36 QA attempts across the 21 stories (all eventually passing), and filed 35 issues: 6 critical, 15 high, 9 medium, 5 low.
.code_my_spec/campaigns/dev_story/synthesis.md:25:The specs themselves had bugs, six distinct classes of them. Two stories specced opposite behavior for the same situation; a spec agent refused to paper over it: "worth a decision on which behavior is authoritative before implementation." Five files had wrong dollar math versus their own gherkin. A shared regex assumed integer job IDs while jobs use UUIDs, so story 846 read 0/5 against a fully correct implementation until the orchestrator fixed the test helper.
.code_my_spec/campaigns/dev_story/synthesis.md:47:Then the environment melted down again, differently. Assets started 404ing mid-QA, the login page 500ed, and arbitrary modules went "not available" on some requests but not others. The QA agent escalated correctly: "this reads as the running release having a partially-loaded/inconsistent code path, not something for me to route around." Root cause: two zombie phx.server processes squatting the port, serving stale partial builds while implementers recompiled underneath. The orchestrator's fix was a new discipline invented mid-run: serve QA from an immutable `mix release` copy, rebuilt after each fix batch, a pattern that held for the rest of the build. Cost of the outage: about 40 minutes, zero John involvement.
.code_my_spec/campaigns/dev_story/synthesis.md:67:July 9 was the shipping day: 16 commits total, the initial commit at 14:19 UTC and 15 more behind it. John's messages shifted to delegation and credentials. "Check @../devops/ and get us a uat deploy of this" produced a Kamal-on-Hetzner deployment in about 75 minutes, including three consecutive deploy failures, each self-diagnosed: the agent had wrongly stripped npm steps from the Dockerfile ("package.json existed all along", it admitted, "my earlier check was wrong"), then a missing health route, then `force_ssl` 301ing the health probe.
.code_my_spec/campaigns/dev_story/synthesis.md:75:The last act came after midnight. John: "Dude you need to get that form testable... you need to get that tested and recording with reqcassette." The resulting cassette-backed Stripe tests found a real security hole within 15 minutes: webhook signature verification had no timestamp tolerance, so a correctly signed payload from a year earlier was accepted. It had been live on UAT. The fix, plus a deploy regression the health check caught safely (a test-only dependency pin broke the production boot path; the old container kept serving), closed the build at 331 tests and 143 specs green, July 10, 01:25 UTC.

content.text:
# run_provisioning_step

Run one named provisioning step directly, skipping the sequence's own
halt-on-first-failure ordering.

`run_devops_setup` walks `Sequence.for_options/1` in order and halts at the
first step that is not done — the ordering *is* the dependency model, so a
step later in the sequence normally has no business running before an
earlier one does. That stops being true the moment an earlier step is
blocked for a reason that has nothing to do with whether later steps can
actually succeed: `:repository` and `:secrets` need to run real commands
against a local checkout, which nothing reached through the light harness
(`/mcp/harness`) can currently do — so they read "missing" indefinitely
regardless of whether the account's real infrastructure (`:server`,
`:domain`, `:dns`, and anything else that is purely a provider API call) is
actually fine. Waiting on the sequence to reach them means never verifying
the parts that already work.

This is the same `run_step/3` `run_devops_setup` and `adopt_repository`
both already use underneath — verified against the provider first, same
`RunLock` respected, same honest outcome reported back. It does not bypass
a step's own verification; it only bypasses *ordering*. Running `:deploy`
before `:server` genuinely exists is still that step's problem to refuse,
not this tool's to prevent.

## `inbound_probe_to` is the other gap `adopt_repository` already had

`Steps.run(:inbound, ...)` already accepts `opts[:inbound_probe_to]` — an
address on the project's own domain to prove receiving actually works,
since Resend accepts mail only to addresses configured for the domain and
offers no way to ask which those are. This tool never exposed a way to
supply one, so the step paused indefinitely asking for something a caller
had no parameter to give it — the same shape as `adopt_repository`'s
missing `:owner` before it could name an organisation's repository.

## `confirm_apex_repoint` is the same gap, for `:dns`

`Steps.apex_repoint/4` refuses to move a live apex onto a freshly created
server without `opts[:confirm_apex_repoint]` — reasonable, since the apex
might be serving real traffic today. But that flag was only ever threaded
from `CodeMySpecWeb.ProvisioningLive`'s own `"confirm_apex_repoint"` event,
so an agent driving this tool instead of a human clicking a button had no
way to say yes: every retry re-detected the live apex and paused again,
identically, with `devops_status` never explaining why nothing progressed.
Confirmed live: a prod cutover the operator had already approved sat paused
through repeated retries because the only "confirm" that existed was a
LiveView click nothing here could reach.

## The `:server` step never creates a server here, under any circumstance

`Steps.server_creation_gate/3` used to accept `opts[:confirm_new_server]`
as a way to create a brand-new server for an unlinked environment anyway —
removed after `broken-oaths-uat` and `broken-oaths-prod` got created by
accident this way instead of sharing the account's existing
`fuellytics`/`fuellytics-prod` boxes. There is no escape hatch left: an
unlinked environment's `:server` step always pauses, naming what the
account would need to link first. Only `Steps.provision_account_server/3`,
reached through the account-level provisioning tool, may create one.

## This returns as soon as the step starts, not when it finishes

Same reason `run_devops_setup` already documents this, for the same
underlying cost: `:deploy` alone has measured ~167s, far longer than the
code-mode sandbox's own 30s wall clock. This used to call `Provisioning.
run_step/2` and wait, which is exactly the shape `run_step_async/3`'s own
moduledoc describes as unsurvivable — confirmed live running `:deploy`
against a harness-only project: every call was brutally killed at 30s with
no trace of what it had started, indistinguishable from a hang. `RunLock`
is what makes "started or refused" the only two outcomes here, the same
handshake `Resources.fix_async/2` uses: the spawned task claims the lock
and only then acks this call, so "started" means the run genuinely holds
it. Call `devops_status` afterward to watch it converge.

## Arguments

  step (string, required)
  confirm_apex_repoint (boolean)
  force (boolean)
  inbound_probe_to (string)

## Example

```lua
local result, err = run_provisioning_step({ step = "…" })
if result == nil then return "failed: " .. err.message end
return result
```

# link_server

Point a project's environment at a server the account already owns.

`provisioning_environments` used to only ever get a server the setup step
created for it — `server_name`/`ip` filled in as it went. An account-level
server (`/app/servers`, story 879) can predate any project that ends up on
it, or serve more than one at once, and nothing connected the two. This is
that connection: once linked, the server step resolves this environment's
box by the linked server's real name instead of deriving one from the
project, so setup finds the box that's actually there rather than one that
was never going to exist under a guessed name.

Link the account's server first (`/app/servers`, or however it's linked)
before calling this — it only points an environment at a server this
account already has a record of.

## Arguments

  environment (string, required)
  server_name (string, required)

## Example

```lua
local result, err = link_server({ server_name = "…", environment = "…" })
if result == nil then return "failed: " .. err.message end
return result
```

# ensure_environment

Create or update a deployment environment row for a project.

`provisioning_environments` are rows, not an enum — a project starts with
none and gets `prod`/`uat`/whatever it needs added. `EnvironmentRepository.
list/1` only seeds the initial `prod`+`uat` pair when a project's row set is
completely empty, so a project that already has one legacy row (adopted
before its devops level was set, or left over from an earlier drill) never
gets a later-needed one created automatically — `permitted_environment_rows/1`
then filters that lone row out for a devops level it doesn't match, and every
step that fans out over environments finds none (`402f9439`).

This is the manual escape hatch: name the environment a project needs and
it exists, the same shape `ProvisioningLive`'s own environment form writes.
Host/server/IP are filled in by the domain/server steps as they provision,
not required here — an empty environment is a valid starting point.

## Arguments

  name (string, required)

## Example

```lua
local result, err = ensure_environment({ name = "…" })
if result == nil then return "failed: " .. err.message end
return result
```

# list_problems

The findings behind the alert, for the agent that wants them.

`Hooks.AnalysisAlert` puts a count and an age on every tool call and stops
there — a finding list on every call is noise the model learns to skip, which
costs the signal a second time and more permanently than never sending it. So
the alert pushes the fact and this pulls the detail, and the split only works
because asking is one tool call.

## Paginated, and not optionally

This working copy holds over 400 credo findings. An unpaginated list would
overflow the tool-response window for the same reason the alert is counts-only
— and a tool that dies on a large project is one nobody can rely on when a
project gets large, which is exactly when they need it.

Defaults to the first page and to `error` severity, because the common case is
"what is blocking me" rather than "everything anyone has ever noticed".

Scoped to the working copy, like everything else keyed on the harness: these
are the findings from *this* checkout's analyzers, not the project's.

## Arguments

  page (integer)
  per_page (integer)
  severity (string)
  source (string)

## Example

```lua
local result, err = list_problems({})
if result == nil then return "failed: " .. err.message end
return result
```

.code_my_spec/campaigns/dev_story/synthesis.md:73:Then, at 21:42, John relayed a third-party tester's findings, prefaced with "I was a little obnoxious to test a few things." In roughly ten minutes of hostile clicking, the tester found what 36 QA passes had not: every quote combination returned "We can't price this yet" (John's own signup test had created an empty account that silently stole the public storefront, which the agent admitted was "a design flaw my earlier single-account assumption papered over"); `ThisManAteMySon@Fartmail.com` was accepted as a valid email; 1 square foot priced at $0.12 with the weekly discount; a 4,000-hour-per-week cleaning was bookable; and there was no payment field yet on the final step. Happy-path QA, even 36 rounds of it, is not adversarial QA. Three agents fixed, migrated, deployed, and browser-verified all findings in about 51 minutes.
.code_my_spec/architecture/proposal.md:5:Authentication (`CleanerCrm.Users`), multi-tenant accounts (`CleanerCrm.Accounts` — the account is the cleaning company/tenant), and OAuth integrations (`CleanerCrm.Integrations`) already exist from the phx.gen.auth / cms_gen generators and are referenced as dependencies, not re-proposed here.

.code_my_spec/architecture/proposal.md:19:- CleanerCrm.Clients.AccessDetail (schema) [Stories: 832]: Entry method, lockbox/alarm codes, and emergency contact for a property, with day-of-job visibility rules

.code_my_spec/architecture/proposal.md:30:- CleanerCrm.Scheduling.RecurringPlan (schema) [Stories: 833, 846]: A weekly/biweekly/monthly plan that generates jobs and records the client's preferred cleaner
.code_my_spec/architecture/proposal.md:31:- CleanerCrm.Scheduling.AvailabilityBlock (schema) [Stories: 833]: A period when a cleaner is unavailable for assignment
.code_my_spec/architecture/proposal.md:32:- CleanerCrm.Scheduling.Recurrence (module) [Stories: 833]: Generates job series from a plan's cadence

# generate_deploy_files

Write the deploy artifacts a project is missing, onto its own checkout.

The same write `ProvisioningLive`'s "Generate deploy files" button performs
— `DeployArtifacts.generate/2`, which never overwrites a file already there.
Exists as its own tool, not folded into `run_devops_setup`, because it is not
an ordered step: nothing in the sequence runs it, `devops_status`'s
deploy-readiness audit only reads what it should have produced, and an agent
that has just read "missing lib/<app>/release.ex" from that audit needs a way
to put it there without a browser.

Writes onto the checkout of whichever project this call is connected to —
no `project_id` parameter, so there is nothing for a caller to name (or
mis-name) a different project's tree with.

## Arguments

  none

## Example

```lua
local result, err = generate_deploy_files({})
if result == nil then return "failed: " .. err.message end
return result
```

1	#!/usr/bin/env bash
2	#
3	#   bin/deploy [uat|prod]              — for a human: push, wait for CI,
4	#                                         migrate, then swap.
5	#   bin/deploy migrate|swap <uat|prod> — what CodeMySpec's own setup
6	#                                         calls. It already built and
7	#                                         pushed a specific image and
8	#                                         drives health checking itself
9	#                                         between the two phases, so
10	#                                         neither is meant to run alone
11	#                                         by hand.
12	set -euo pipefail
13	
14	case "${1:-}" in
15	  migrate|swap)
16	    PHASE="$1"
17	    ENVIRONMENT="${2:?usage: bin/deploy $1 <uat|prod>}"
18	    ;;
19	  *)
20	    PHASE="all"
21	    ENVIRONMENT="${1:-uat}"
22	    ;;
23	esac
24	
25	CONFIG="config/deploy.yml"
26	[ "$ENVIRONMENT" = "uat" ] && CONFIG="config/deploy.uat.yml"
27	
28	# CMS_IMAGE names the exact image (registry/repo:tag) setup already built
29	# and pushed. Building or pulling another one here would deploy a
30	# different commit than the one setup verified. Without it — a human
31	# running this by hand — the version is whatever HEAD names once CI has
32	# published it.
33	if [ -n "${CMS_IMAGE:-}" ]; then
34	  VERSION="${CMS_IMAGE##*:}"
35	else
36	  VERSION="$(git rev-parse HEAD)"
37	fi
38	
39	swap() {
40	  # `--skip-push`: by the time this runs, the image is already on the
41	  # registry — setup's own builder pushed it (the automated path) or
42	  # `wait for CI to publish it` already did (the human "all" path).
43	  # Without this flag, `kamal deploy` rebuilds and re-pushes the image
44	  # itself before pulling it back down, and that redundant push's
45	  # blob-existence check (verifying blobs the FIRST push already
46	  # uploaded) is a different code path in buildx's registry client than
47	  # uploading new content — one that ignores the daemon's
48	  # insecure-registries config and always assumes HTTPS. Confirmed live
49	  # against MarketMySpec: a self-hosted HTTP-only registry accepted the
50	  # first push fine and only failed on kamal's own redundant second one.
51	  kamal deploy --config-file "$CONFIG" --version "$VERSION" --skip-push
52	}
53	
54	migrate() {
55	  # `-e`, so the migration carries the key instead of reading the host's
56	  # copy. `kamal app exec` loads env/roles/<role>.env from the host, and
57	  # kamal writes that only when it boots a container — so the migration
58	  # ran against the environment of the last successful boot. A rotated
59	  # SOPS_AGE_KEY deadlocked on it: the deploy re-encrypts to the new key,
60	  # the migration reads the old one off the host, and the deploy that
61	  # would replace the host's copy is the one that cannot finish.
62	  #
63	  # `--config-file`, not `--config` — kamal has no `--config` flag at
64	  # all, only `-c`/`--config-file`. Thor silently folded the unrecognised
65	  # `--config "$CONFIG"` into `app exec`'s own CMD positional, so runc
66	  # tried to exec the literal string "--config" as the container's
67	  # entrypoint. Confirmed live against MarketMySpec on kamal 2.11.0.
68	  #
69	  # A host with no successful deploy in its history has no env file at
70	  # all yet — kamal only ever writes one as a side effect of booting a
71	  # container. `CodeMySpec.Provisioning.Deploy.run/3` is what handles
72	  # that case (an explicit, logged "bootstrap" phase before retrying

#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
#   bin/deploy [uat|prod]              — for a human: push, wait for CI,
#                                         migrate, then swap.
#   bin/deploy migrate|swap <uat|prod> — what CodeMySpec's own setup
#                                         calls. It already built and
#                                         pushed a specific image and
#                                         drives health checking itself
#                                         between the two phases, so
#                                         neither is meant to run alone
#                                         by hand.
set -euo pipefail

case "${1:-}" in
  migrate|swap)
    PHASE="$1"
    ENVIRONMENT="${2:?usage: bin/deploy $1 <uat|prod>}"
    ;;
  *)
    PHASE="all"
    ENVIRONMENT="${1:-uat}"
    ;;
esac

CONFIG="config/deploy.yml"
[ "$ENVIRONMENT" = "uat" ] && CONFIG="config/deploy.uat.yml"

# CMS_IMAGE names the exact image (registry/repo:tag) setup already built
# and pushed. Building or pulling another one here would deploy a
# different commit than the one setup verified. Without it — a human
# running this by hand — the version is whatever HEAD names once CI has
# published it.
if [ -n "${CMS_IMAGE:-}" ]; then
  VERSION="${CMS_IMAGE##*:}"
else
  VERSION="$(git rev-parse HEAD)"
fi

swap() {
  # `--skip-push`: by the time this runs, the image is already on the
  # registry — setup's own builder pushed it (the automated path) or
  # `wait for CI to publish it` already did (the human "all" path).
  # Without this flag, `kamal deploy` rebuilds and re-pushes the image
  # itself before pulling it back down, and that redundant push's
  # blob-existence check (verifying blobs the FIRST push already
  # uploaded) is a different code path in buildx's registry client than
  # uploading new content — one that ignores the daemon's
  # insecure-registries config and always assumes HTTPS. Confirmed live
  # against MarketMySpec: a self-hosted HTTP-only registry accepted the
  # first push fine and only failed on kamal's own redundant second one.
  kamal deploy --config-file "$CONFIG" --version "$VERSION" --skip-push
}

migrate() {
  # `-e`, so the migration carries the key instead of reading the host's
  # copy. `kamal app exec` loads env/roles/<role>.env from the host, and
  # kamal writes that only when it boots a container — so the migration
  # ran against the environment of the last successful boot. A rotated
  # SOPS_AGE_KEY deadlocked on it: the deploy re-encrypts to the new key,
  # the migration reads the old one off the host, and the deploy that
  # would replace the host's copy is the one that cannot finish.
  #
  # `--config-file`, not `--config` — kamal has no `--config` flag at
  # all, only `-c`/`--config-file`. Thor silently folded the unrecognised
  # `--config "$CONFIG"` into `app exec`'s own CMD positional, so runc
  # tried to exec the literal string "--config" as the container's
  # entrypoint. Confirmed live against MarketMySpec on kamal 2.11.0.
  #
  # A host with no successful deploy in its history has no env file at
  # all yet — kamal only ever writes one as a side effect of booting a
  # container. `CodeMySpec.Provisioning.Deploy.run/3` is what handles
  # that case (an explicit, logged "bootstrap" phase before retrying
  # migrate), not this script: `bin/deploy migrate` just fails here, the
  # same as any other migrate failure, and the caller decides what a
  # missing env file means.
  kamal app exec --config-file "$CONFIG" --version "$VERSION" -e "SOPS_AGE_KEY:${SOPS_AGE_KEY:-}" "bin/migrate"
}

case "$PHASE" in
  migrate)
    migrate
    ;;
  swap)
    swap
    ;;
  all)
    echo "deploying $VERSION to $ENVIRONMENT"

    git push origin HEAD

    echo "waiting for CI to publish the image for $VERSION"
    gh run watch --exit-status "$(gh run list --commit "$VERSION" --limit 1 --json databaseId --jq '.[0].databaseId')"

    migrate
    swap

    echo "deployed $VERSION to $ENVIRONMENT"
    ;;
esac

# Hetzner + Kamal Deployment

Reference for provisioning Hetzner Cloud servers and deploying a Phoenix/Elixir app with **Kamal 2**. Images are built in CI and pushed to GHCR; Kamal pulls them onto the host and **kamal-proxy** terminates TLS and routes by hostname. App secrets come from AWS SSM at boot.

**Stack:** Hetzner cax11 (ARM64) / shared-vCPU (amd64), Ubuntu 24.04, Kamal 2 + kamal-proxy, Postgres 17 (shared `infra-postgres-1` container on a `db_net` network), GHCR for images, AWS SSM Parameter Store for secrets.

> **History:** this project deployed with Docker Compose + Caddy + rsync until early 2026. Both `market_my_spec` and `get_ai_traffic` migrated to the Kamal stack below. If you find a `docker-compose.prod.yml` + `Caddyfile` in a repo, it's vestigial — the live path is `scripts/deploy` → Kamal.

Companion playbooks:
- `ci-image-build.md` — the GitHub Actions multi-arch build that produces the GHCR image this deploy pulls.
- `secrets-ssm.md` — Varlock (local) → SSM Parameter Store (prod) secret lifecycle that `.kamal/secrets-common` and `Secrets.load!/1` depend on.
- `aws-s3-iam.md` — the IAM user (S3 + SSM) the running container uses.

Sources:
- [Kamal docs](https://kamal-deploy.org/)
- [kamal-proxy](https://github.com/basecamp/kamal-proxy)
- [hcloud CLI](https://github.com/hetznercloud/cli/releases)
- [Phoenix releases guide](https://hexdocs.pm/phoenix/releases.html)

---

## 1. Hetzner Cloud CLI (hcloud)

### Installation

```bash
# macOS
brew install hcloud

# Linux
curl -fsSL https://github.com/hetznercloud/cli/releases/latest/download/hcloud-linux-amd64.tar.gz | tar xz
sudo mv hcloud /usr/local/bin/

# Authenticate — paste API token from Hetzner console
hcloud context create myproject
```

### SSH Key Management

```bash
hcloud ssh-key create --name my-key --public-key-from-file ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
hcloud ssh-key list
hcloud ssh-key delete my-key
```

### Server Provisioning

cax11 is an ARM64 (Ampere Altra) shared-vCPU plan: 2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM, 40 GB SSD, ~3.79 EUR/month, EU regions only (fsn1, nbg1, hel1). A `cx`/`cpx` amd64 plan works too — match the box arch to the image arch you build in CI (`builder.arch` in `config/deploy.yml`).

```bash
hcloud server-type list
hcloud image list --type system | grep ubuntu

hcloud server create \
  --name myproject-prod \
  --type cax11 \
  --image ubuntu-24.04 \
  --location fsn1 \
  --ssh-key my-key \
  --firewall myproject-fw

hcloud server describe myproject-prod | grep "Public Net"
ssh root@<IP>
```

### Firewall Rules

kamal-proxy listens on 80/443. Open those plus SSH.

```bash
hcloud firewall create --name myproject-fw

# SSH from your IP only
hcloud firewall add-rule myproject-fw \
  --direction in --source-ips YOUR_IP/32 --protocol tcp --port 22

# HTTP (ACME HTTP-01 challenge) + HTTPS + HTTP/3
hcloud firewall add-rule myproject-fw --direction in --source-ips 0.0.0.0/0 --source-ips ::/0 --protocol tcp --port 80
hcloud firewall add-rule myproject-fw --direction in --source-ips 0.0.0.0/0 --source-ips ::/0 --protocol tcp --port 443
hcloud firewall add-rule myproject-fw --direction in --source-ips 0.0.0.0/0 --source-ips ::/0 --protocol udp --port 443
```

### Snapshots

Take a snapshot before risky operations (OS upgrades, major migrations). ~0.01 EUR/GB/month.

```bash
hcloud server create-image myproject-prod --type snapshot \
  --description "Before Postgres 17 upgrade $(date +%Y-%m-%d)"
hcloud image list --type snapshot
```

---

## 2. Server Bootstrap (one-time)

Kamal installs Docker itself on first deploy (`kamal server bootstrap`), but for a shared box you provision the Postgres container and the shared network once.

```bash
# Update + Docker (kamal will also do this; harmless if pre-installed)
apt-get update && apt-get upgrade -y
curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sh
docker compose version

# Shared app network — every app's container attaches here to reach Postgres.
docker network create db_net

# Shared Postgres (one per host, all apps use their own DB + per-app user).
docker run -d --name infra-postgres-1 --restart unless-stopped \
  --network db_net \
  -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=<superuser-pw> \
  -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data \
  postgres:17
```

Kamal connects over SSH as `root` (`ssh: { user: root }` in `config/deploy.yml`). Hardening (key-only SSH, fail2ban, unattended-upgrades) is in §9; in practice these and the Postgres provisioning live in a shared **`devops/` monorepo**, not in each app repo.

---

## 3. The Kamal Deploy Model

One `config/deploy.yml` per environment. kamal-proxy (started automatically) owns :80/:443, terminates TLS via Let's Encrypt, and routes by `Host` — so multiple apps coexist on one box with no shared Caddy and no `COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME`.

```yaml
# config/deploy.yml (prod)
service: myapp
image: code-my-spec/myapp           # GHCR repo (registry.server prepended)

servers:
  web:
    hosts:
      - <PROD_IP>
    options:
      network: db_net               # pre-attach so the container can reach infra-postgres-1 at boot

proxy:
  ssl: true                         # kamal-proxy gets a Let's Encrypt cert for `host`
  host: myapp.com
  app_port: 4000
  healthcheck:
    path: /health                   # gates the traffic swap (see §6)

registry:
  server: ghcr.io
  username: johns10
  password:
    - KAMAL_REGISTRY_PASSWORD       # = `gh auth token`, exported by scripts/deploy

builder:
  arch: amd64                       # match the host arch; arm64 for cax11 boxes
  local: true                      # not actually invoked — deploys use --skip-push (CI built the image)

env:
  clear:
    APP_ENV: prod                   # runtime env discriminator (see secrets-ssm.md)
    AWS_REGION: us-east-1
  secret:
    - AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID             # bootstrap creds only — app secrets come from SSM at boot
    - AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY

ssh:
  user: root
```

Key facts:
- **No Caddy, no Compose.** kamal-proxy is the reverse proxy. A `Caddyfile` in the repo is reference-only.
- **`options.network: db_net`** attaches the container to the shared network at create time so `DATABASE_URL=ecto://...@infra-postgres-1/myapp_prod` resolves.
- **`env.secret` carries only AWS bootstrap creds** (+ the GHCR token). Every other secret is fetched from SSM at boot — see `secrets-ssm.md`.
- **`APP_ENV`** (not `MIX_ENV`) selects prod vs uat at runtime, so one `MIX_ENV=prod` image serves both.

### Multi-environment

Separate boxes, one `config/deploy.<env>.yml` each (e.g. `config/deploy.uat.yml` → `<UAT_IP>`, `host: uat.myapp.com`, `APP_ENV: uat`, often `arch: arm64`). This replaces the old single-host `COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME` split — isolation is physical, and each box can co-host unrelated apps (prod box also runs `market_my_spec`; uat box also runs `fuellytics`).

---

## 4. Image Build (CI)

Images are **not** built on the deploy machine. GitHub Actions builds a multi-arch image on push to `master` and pushes it to GHCR tagged with the commit SHA. `scripts/deploy` waits for that build, then `kamal deploy --skip-push --version=<sha>` pulls it. Full detail: **`ci-image-build.md`**.

---

## 5. Deployment Workflow

`scripts/deploy` is the only supported entry point — never run `kamal deploy` directly (the bootstrap creds must be rendered from SSM first).

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/deploy — deploy prod
set -euo pipefail
REPO_ROOT=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd); cd "$REPO_ROOT"
DEVOPS_DIR="${DEVOPS_DIR:-$HOME/Documents/github/devops}"

# 1. Clean tree (Kamal versions by commit SHA)
[[ -z "$(git status --porcelain)" ]] || { echo "commit/stash first" >&2; git status --short >&2; exit 1; }
SHA=$(git rev-parse HEAD); BRANCH=$(git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD)

# 2. Push and wait for the CI build to land in GHCR
git push origin "$BRANCH"
sleep 5
RUN_ID=$(gh run list --workflow=build.yml --branch="$BRANCH" --limit=1 --json databaseId --jq '.[0].databaseId')
gh run watch "$RUN_ID" --exit-status --interval 10

# 3. GHCR pull token + render AWS bootstrap creds from SSM into a temp file
export KAMAL_REGISTRY_PASSWORD; KAMAL_REGISTRY_PASSWORD=$(gh auth token)
ENV_FILE=$(mktemp); trap 'rm -f "$ENV_FILE"' EXIT
"$DEVOPS_DIR/scripts/render-env" myapp prod --out "$ENV_FILE" || { echo "render-env failed; run 'aws sso login'" >&2; exit 1; }
set -a; source "$ENV_FILE"; set +a
unset AWS_SESSION_TOKEN AWS_SECURITY_TOKEN AWS_PROFILE     # container needs the long-term IAM pair, not your SSO STS token
for r in AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY; do
  [[ -n "${!r:-}" ]] || { echo "ERROR: $r empty after render-env; refusing to deploy" >&2; exit 1; }
done

# 4. Migrate against the NEW image BEFORE swapping traffic
kamal app exec --version="$SHA" "/app/bin/migrate"

# 5. Swap traffic
kamal deploy --skip-push --version="$SHA" "$@"
```

> **Why the temp-file + hard-fail guard (steps 3):** `source <(render-env ...)` (process substitution) swallows `render-env`'s exit code. If SSO is stale it prints nothing, `source` consumes nothing, and the deploy proceeds with **empty** AWS keys — Kamal then pushes an empty env-file to the host that survives across every later `kamal app exec`, bricking prod secrets. Render to a temp file, check the exit code, and refuse to deploy on empty creds.

### First deploy per environment (bootstrap)

The migrate-before-swap order assumes Kamal's per-host env-file already exists. On a brand-new env it doesn't, so the very first deploy is manual:

```bash
kamal deploy --skip-push --version=<sha> -c config/deploy.yml
kamal app exec --version=<sha> -c config/deploy.yml /app/bin/migrate
```

Thereafter use `scripts/deploy`.

---

## 6. Migrations & Health

### Migrate before traffic swap

`kamal app exec --version=<sha> /app/bin/migrate` boots a one-off container from the **new** image, runs migrations, and exits. The currently-serving (old) container keeps handling traffic against the now-migrated schema until `kamal deploy` swaps it in.

`bin/migrate` is a release overlay (`rel/overlays/bin/migrate`):

```sh
#!/bin/sh
set -eu
cd -P -- "$(dirname -- "$0")"
exec ./myapp eval MyApp.Release.migrate
```

> **Additive-only constraint:** during the migrate-then-swap window the **old** code runs against the **new** schema. A destructive migration (drop column the old code still reads) breaks the old container in that gap. Two-phase it: deploy code that stops reading the column, then a later deploy that drops it.

### Health endpoint

kamal-proxy gates the swap on `proxy.healthcheck.path`. Define it **outside all router pipelines** (no session, CSRF, auth, or DB):

```elixir
# router.ex
scope "/", MyAppWeb do
  get "/health", PageController, :health   # no :browser / :api pipeline
end
# page_controller.ex
def health(conn, _params), do: send_resp(conn, 200, "ok")
```

**`force_ssl` gotcha:** kamal-proxy's internal health probe hits the app port directly (plain HTTP, no `X-Forwarded-Proto`). If you use `force_ssl`, exclude the health path or it 301s and the probe fails:

```elixir
config :myapp, MyAppWeb.Endpoint,
  force_ssl: [rewrite_on: [:x_forwarded_proto], exclude: ["/up", "localhost", "127.0.0.1"]]
```

(`get_ai_traffic` uses `/health` and reports no exclusion needed; `market_my_spec` uses `/up` and excludes it. Match the path to your proxy config and test the probe.)

---

## 7. Secrets

`.kamal/secrets-common` is a Dotenv file Kamal reads; `${VAR}` tokens are interpolated from the deploy shell (populated by `scripts/deploy`). **It carries only bootstrap creds — never app secrets:**

```bash
# .kamal/secrets-common
KAMAL_REGISTRY_PASSWORD=${KAMAL_REGISTRY_PASSWORD}
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=${AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID}
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=${AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY}
```

At container boot, `MyApp.Secrets.load!/1` pulls everything under `/myapp/<APP_ENV>/` from SSM into the OS env before `runtime.exs` reads it. Full lifecycle (Varlock locally, SSM in prod, seeding, rotation): **`secrets-ssm.md`**.

---

## 8. Database Management

DB is the shared `infra-postgres-1` container on `db_net`, with a per-app database and per-app user (e.g. `myapp_prod_app`). `DATABASE_URL` is an SSM param.

```bash
# Manual dump (run on the host)
docker exec infra-postgres-1 pg_dump -U myapp_prod_app myapp_prod | gzip > /opt/backups/myapp-prod-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S).sql.gz

# Restore
gunzip -c backup.sql.gz | docker exec -i infra-postgres-1 psql -U myapp_prod_app myapp_prod
```

In practice, scheduled `pg_dump` cron + retention purge live in the shared **`devops/` monorepo** (one backup job for the shared Postgres), not per-app.

---

## 9. Server Hardening

Typically applied once per host from the shared `devops/` monorepo.

```bash
# /etc/ssh/sshd_config — key-only
PermitRootLogin prohibit-password
PasswordAuthentication no
PubkeyAuthentication yes
```

```bash
# fail2ban
apt-get install -y fail2ban
printf '[sshd]\nenabled = true\nbantime = 3600\nfindtime = 600\nmaxretry = 5\n' > /etc/fail2ban/jail.local
systemctl enable --now fail2ban

# unattended upgrades
apt-get install -y unattended-upgrades && dpkg-reconfigure -plow unattended-upgrades
```

> Docker bypasses UFW by writing its own iptables rules. The **Hetzner cloud firewall** (network edge, §1) is the reliable control for inbound access. kamal-proxy publishes 80/443; nothing else should be exposed.

---

## 10. Operational Runbook

Kamal is the primary tool — most ops don't need a raw SSH session.

```bash
# Status / logs
kamal app details
kamal app logs -f
kamal app logs --grep ERROR

# Shell / IEx in the running container
kamal app exec -i --reuse "/app/bin/myapp remote"

# One-off command against current version
kamal app exec "/app/bin/myapp eval ':ok'"

# Rollback to a previous SHA (image still in GHCR)
kamal rollback <old-sha>

# kamal-proxy state (routes, certs)
kamal proxy details
```

### Common Issues

**Every request 500s right after a "successful" deploy** — migrations didn't run before the swap. Confirm `scripts/deploy` ran `kamal app exec --version=$SHA /app/bin/migrate` *before* `kamal deploy`.

**Container boots then exits / "No SSM parameters found"** — bootstrap AWS creds are empty or the IAM user can't read `/myapp/<env>/*`. Check `secrets-ssm.md` and the IAM policy in `aws-s3-iam.md`. Re-run `aws sso login`.

**kamal-proxy health probe fails / endless redirect** — `force_ssl` is 301-ing the health path. Exclude it (§6).

**`DATABASE_URL`/host unreachable** — the container isn't on `db_net`. Confirm `servers.web.options.network: db_net` and that `infra-postgres-1` is running on the same network.

**Deploy proceeds with empty AWS keys** — you bypassed `scripts/deploy` or used process substitution for `render-env`. Always go through the script (§5).

```yaml
      - <PROD_IP>
    options:
      network: db_net               # pre-attach so the container can reach infra-postgres-1 at boot

proxy:
  ssl: true                         # kamal-proxy gets a Let's Encrypt cert for `host`
  host: myapp.com
  app_port: 4000
  healthcheck:
    path: /health                   # gates the traffic swap (see §6)

registry:
  server: ghcr.io
  username: johns10
  password:
    - KAMAL_REGISTRY_PASSWORD       # = `gh auth token`, exported by scripts/deploy

builder:
  arch: amd64                       # match the host arch; arm64 for cax11 boxes
  local: true                      # not actually invoked — deploys use --skip-push (CI built the image)

env:
  clear:
    APP_ENV: prod                   # runtime env discriminator (see secrets-ssm.md)
    AWS_REGION: us-east-1
  secret:
    - AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID             # bootstrap creds only — app secrets come from SSM at boot
    - AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY

ssh:
  user: root
```

Key facts:
- **No Caddy, no Compose.** kamal-proxy is the reverse proxy. A `Caddyfile` in the repo is reference-only.
- **`options.network: db_net`** attaches the container to the shared network at create time so `DATABASE_URL=ecto://...@infra-postgres-1/myapp_prod` resolves.
- **`env.secret` carries only AWS bootstrap creds** (+ the GHCR token). Every other secret is fetched from SSM at boot — see `secrets-ssm.md`.
- **`APP_ENV`** (not `MIX_ENV`) selects prod vs uat at runtime, so one `MIX_ENV=prod` image serves both.

### Multi-environment

Separate boxes, one `config/deploy.<env>.yml` each (e.g. `config/deploy.uat.yml` → `<UAT_IP>`, `host: uat.myapp.com`, `APP_ENV: uat`, often `arch: arm64`). This replaces the old single-host `COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME` split — isolation is physical, and each box can co-host unrelated apps (prod box also runs `market_my_spec`; uat box also runs `fuellytics`).

---

## 4. Image Build (CI)

Images are **not** built on the deploy machine. GitHub Actions builds a multi-arch image on push to `master` and pushes it to GHCR tagged with the commit SHA. `scripts/deploy` waits for that build, then `kamal deploy --skip-push --version=<sha>` pulls it. Full detail: **`ci-image-build.md`**.

---

## 5. Deployment Workflow

`scripts/deploy` is the only supported entry point — never run `kamal deploy` directly (the bootstrap creds must be rendered from SSM first).

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/deploy — deploy prod
set -euo pipefail
REPO_ROOT=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd); cd "$REPO_ROOT"
DEVOPS_DIR="${DEVOPS_DIR:-$HOME/Documents/github/devops}"

# 1. Clean tree (Kamal versions by commit SHA)
[[ -z "$(git status --porcelain)" ]] || { echo "commit/stash first" >&2; git status --short >&2; exit 1; }
SHA=$(git rev-parse HEAD); BRANCH=$(git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD)

# 2. Push and wait for the CI build to land in GHCR
git push origin "$BRANCH"
sleep 5
RUN_ID=$(gh run list --workflow=build.yml --branch="$BRANCH" --limit=1 --json databaseId --jq '.[0].databaseId')
gh run watch "$RUN_ID" --exit-status --interval 10

# 3. GHCR pull token + render AWS bootstrap creds from SSM into a temp file
export KAMAL_REGISTRY_PASSWORD; KAMAL_REGISTRY_PASSWORD=$(gh auth token)
ENV_FILE=$(mktemp); trap 'rm -f "$ENV_FILE"' EXIT
"$DEVOPS_DIR/scripts/render-env" myapp prod --out "$ENV_FILE" || { echo "render-env failed; run 'aws sso login'" >&2; exit 1; }
set -a; source "$ENV_FILE"; set +a
unset AWS_SESSION_TOKEN AWS_SECURITY_TOKEN AWS_PROFILE     # container needs the long-term IAM pair, not your SSO STS token
for r in AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY; do
  [[ -n "${!r:-}" ]] || { echo "ERROR: $r empty after render-env; refusing to deploy" >&2; exit 1; }
done

# 4. Migrate against the NEW image BEFORE swapping traffic
kamal app exec --version="$SHA" "/app/bin/migrate"

# 5. Swap traffic
kamal deploy --skip-push --version="$SHA" "$@"
```

> **Why the temp-file + hard-fail guard (steps 3):** `source <(render-env ...)` (process substitution) swallows `render-env`'s exit code. If SSO is stale it prints nothing, `source` consumes nothing, and the deploy proceeds with **empty** AWS keys — Kamal then pushes an empty env-file to the host that survives across every later `kamal app exec`, bricking prod secrets. Render to a temp file, check the exit code, and refuse to deploy on empty creds.

### First deploy per environment (bootstrap)

The migrate-before-swap order assumes Kamal's per-host env-file already exists. On a brand-new env it doesn't, so the very first deploy is manual:

```bash
kamal deploy --skip-push --version=<sha> -c config/deploy.yml
kamal app exec --version=<sha> -c config/deploy.yml /app/bin/migrate
```

Thereafter use `scripts/deploy`.

---

## 6. Migrations & Health

### Migrate before traffic swap

`kamal app exec --version=<sha> /app/bin/migrate` boots a one-off container from the **new** image, runs migrations, and exits. The currently-serving (old) container keeps handling traffic against the now-migrated schema until `kamal deploy` swaps it in.

`bin/migrate` is a release overlay (`rel/overlays/bin/migrate`):

```sh
#!/bin/sh
set -eu
cd -P -- "$(dirname -- "$0")"
exec ./myapp eval MyApp.Release.migrate
```

> **Additive-only constraint:** during the migrate-then-swap window the **old** code runs against the **new** schema. A destructive migration (drop column the old code still reads) breaks the old container in that gap. Two-phase it: deploy code that stops reading the column, then a later deploy that drops it.

### Health endpoint

kamal-proxy gates the swap on `proxy.healthcheck.path`. Define it **outside all router pipelines** (no session, CSRF, auth, or DB):

```elixir
# router.ex
scope "/", MyAppWeb do
  get "/health", PageController, :health   # no :browser / :api pipeline
end
# page_controller.ex
def health(conn, _params), do: send_resp(conn, 200, "ok")
```

**`force_ssl` gotcha:** kamal-proxy's internal health probe hits the app port directly (plain HTTP, no `X-Forwarded-Proto`). If you use `force_ssl`, exclude the health path or it 301s and the probe fails:

```elixir
config :myapp, MyAppWeb.Endpoint,
  force_ssl: [rewrite_on: [:x_forwarded_proto], exclude: ["/up", "localhost", "127.0.0.1"]]
```

(`get_ai_traffic` uses `/health` and reports no exclusion needed; `market_my_spec` uses `/up` and excludes it. Match the path to your proxy config and test the probe.)

---

## 7. Secrets

`.kamal/secrets-common` is a Dotenv file Kamal reads; `${VAR}` tokens are interpolated from the deploy shell (populated by `scripts/deploy`). **It carries only bootstrap creds — never app secrets:**

```bash
# .kamal/secrets-common
KAMAL_REGISTRY_PASSWORD=${KAMAL_REGISTRY_PASSWORD}
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=${AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID}
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=${AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY}
```

At container boot, `MyApp.Secrets.load!/1` pulls everything under `/myapp/<APP_ENV>/` from SSM into the OS env before `runtime.exs` reads it. Full lifecycle (Varlock locally, SSM in prod, seeding, rotation): **`secrets-ssm.md`**.

---

## 8. Database Management

DB is the shared `infra-postgres-1` container on `db_net`, with a per-app database and per-app user (e.g. `myapp_prod_app`). `DATABASE_URL` is an SSM param.

```bash
# Manual dump (run on the host)
docker exec infra-postgres-1 pg_dump -U myapp_prod_app myapp_prod | gzip > /opt/backups/myapp-prod-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S).sql.gz

# Restore
gunzip -c backup.sql.gz | docker exec -i infra-postgres-1 psql -U myapp_prod_app myapp_prod
```

In practice, scheduled `pg_dump` cron + retention purge live in the shared **`devops/` monorepo** (one backup job for the shared Postgres), not per-app.

---

## 9. Server Hardening

Typically applied once per host from the shared `devops/` monorepo.

```bash
# /etc/ssh/sshd_config — key-only
PermitRootLogin prohibit-password
PasswordAuthentication no
PubkeyAuthentication yes
```

```bash
# fail2ban
apt-get install -y fail2ban
printf '[sshd]\nenabled = true\nbantime = 3600\nfindtime = 600\nmaxretry = 5\n' > /etc/fail2ban/jail.local
systemctl enable --now fail2ban

# unattended upgrades
apt-get install -y unattended-upgrades && dpkg-reconfigure -plow unattended-upgrades
```

> Docker bypasses UFW by writing its own iptables rules. The **Hetzner cloud firewall** (network edge, §1) is the reliable control for inbound access. kamal-proxy publishes 80/443; nothing else should be exposed.

---

## 10. Operational Runbook

Kamal is the primary tool — most ops don't need a raw SSH session.

```bash
# Status / logs
kamal app details
kamal app logs -f
kamal app logs --grep ERROR

# Shell / IEx in the running container
kamal app exec -i --reuse "/app/bin/myapp remote"

# One-off command against current version
kamal app exec "/app/bin/myapp eval ':ok'"

# Rollback to a previous SHA (image still in GHCR)
kamal rollback <old-sha>

# kamal-proxy state (routes, certs)
kamal proxy details
```

### Common Issues

**Every request 500s right after a "successful" deploy** — migrations didn't run before the swap. Confirm `scripts/deploy` ran `kamal app exec --version=$SHA /app/bin/migrate` *before* `kamal deploy`.

**Container boots then exits / "No SSM parameters found"** — bootstrap AWS creds are empty or the IAM user can't read `/myapp/<env>/*`. Check `secrets-ssm.md` and the IAM policy in `aws-s3-iam.md`. Re-run `aws sso login`.

**kamal-proxy health probe fails / endless redirect** — `force_ssl` is 301-ing the health path. Exclude it (§6).

**`DATABASE_URL`/host unreachable** — the container isn't on `db_net`. Confirm `servers.web.options.network: db_net` and that `infra-postgres-1` is running on the same network.

**Deploy proceeds with empty AWS keys** — you bypassed `scripts/deploy` or used process substitution for `render-env`. Always go through the script (§5).

defmodule CleanerCrmWeb.Router do
  use CleanerCrmWeb, :router

  import CleanerCrmWeb.UserAuth

  pipeline :browser do
    plug :accepts, ["html"]
    plug :fetch_session
    plug :fetch_live_flash
    plug :put_root_layout, html: {CleanerCrmWeb.Layouts, :root}
    plug :protect_from_forgery
    plug :put_secure_browser_headers
    plug :fetch_current_scope_for_user
  end

  pipeline :api do
    plug :accepts, ["json"]
  end

  # No `:protect_from_forgery` — unlike the GET-only public routes below
  # (which can just use `:browser`), `/pay/:token` accepts a POST from a
  # client with no session and no CSRF token (a mailed or shared link).
  # `:fetch_current_scope_for_user` still runs — the root layout reads
  # `@current_scope` unconditionally, and this plug assigns `nil` when
  # no one's logged in rather than requiring an authenticated visitor.
  pipeline :public do
    plug :accepts, ["html"]
    plug :fetch_session
    plug :fetch_flash
    plug :put_root_layout, html: {CleanerCrmWeb.Layouts, :root}
    plug :put_secure_browser_headers
    plug :fetch_current_scope_for_user
  end

  pipeline :webhook do
    plug :accepts, ["json"]
  end

  # Office-only controller routes (e.g. the payroll CSV export) layer
  # this on top of `:require_authenticated_user`; office-only
  # LiveViews use the equivalent `CleanerCrmWeb.RequireOfficeRole`
  # on_mount hook instead, since a plug can't gate a live_session.
  pipeline :require_office_role do
    plug CleanerCrmWeb.RequireOfficeRole
  end

  scope "/", CleanerCrmWeb do
    pipe_through :browser

    get "/", PageController, :home
  end

  # Other scopes may use custom stacks.
  # scope "/api", CleanerCrmWeb do
  #   pipe_through :api

defmodule CleanerCrm.MixProject do
  use Mix.Project

  def project do
    [
      app: :cleaner_crm,
      version: "0.1.0",
      elixir: "~> 1.19",
      elixirc_paths: elixirc_paths(Mix.env()),
      start_permanent: Mix.env() == :prod,
      aliases: aliases(),
      deps: deps(),
      compilers: compilers(Mix.env()),
      listeners: [Phoenix.CodeReloader]
    ]
  end

  # Configuration for the OTP application.
  #
  # Type `mix help compile.app` for more information.
  def application do
    [
      mod: {CleanerCrmWeb.Application, []},
      extra_applications: [:logger, :runtime_tools]
    ]
  end

  def cli do
    [
      preferred_envs: [precommit: :test, spex: :test]
    ]
  end

  defp compilers(:test),
    do: [:diagnostics, :boundary, :phoenix_live_view, :erlang, :elixir, :spex, :app]

  # :diagnostics comes from code_my_spec_generators (a dev-only dep), so
  # prod builds (Docker release) must not list it.
  defp compilers(:prod), do: [:boundary, :phoenix_live_view, :erlang, :elixir, :app]

  defp compilers(_),
    do: [:diagnostics, :boundary, :phoenix_live_view, :erlang, :elixir, :app]

  # Specifies which paths to compile per environment.
  defp elixirc_paths(:test), do: ["lib", "test/support"]
  defp elixirc_paths(_), do: ["lib"]

  # Specifies your project dependencies.
  #
  # Type `mix help deps` for examples and options.
  defp deps do
    [
      {:bcrypt_elixir, "~> 3.0"},
      {:phoenix, "~> 1.8.8"},
      {:phoenix_ecto, "~> 4.5"},
      {:ecto_sql, "~> 3.13"},
      {:postgrex, ">= 0.0.0"},
      {:phoenix_html, "~> 4.1"},
      {:phoenix_live_reload, "~> 1.2", only: :dev},
      {:phoenix_live_view, "~> 1.2.0"},
      {:lazy_html, ">= 0.1.0", only: :test},
      {:phoenix_live_dashboard, "~> 0.8.3"},
      {:esbuild, "~> 0.10", runtime: Mix.env() == :dev},
      {:tailwind, "~> 0.3", runtime: Mix.env() == :dev},
      {:heroicons,
       github: "tailwindlabs/heroicons",
       tag: "v2.2.0",
       sparse: "optimized",
       app: false,
       compile: false,
       depth: 1},
      {:swoosh, "~> 1.16"},
      {:req, "~> 0.5"},
      {:oban, "~> 2.18"},
      {:telemetry_metrics, "~> 1.0"},
      {:telemetry_poller, "~> 1.0"},
      {:gettext, "~> 1.0"},
      {:jason, "~> 1.2"},
      {:dns_cluster, "~> 0.2.0"},
      {:bandit, "~> 1.5"},
      {:assent, "~> 0.3"},
      {:cloak_ecto, "~> 1.3"},
      {:cloak, "~> 1.1"},
      {:credo, "~> 1.7", only: [:dev, :test], runtime: false},
      {:client_utils, "~> 0.1"},
      {:sobelow, "~> 0.13", only: [:dev, :test], runtime: false},
      {:sexy_spex, github: "JediLuke/spex", branch: "main", only: :test},
      # SSM-bootstrap secret loading (CleanerCrm.Secrets) — see the
      # devops repo's SSM pattern. Uses the app's existing Req as the
      # ExAws HTTP client (hackney 4.x is already in the tree via
      # httpoison and conflicts with ExAws's default).
      {:ex_aws, "~> 2.5"},
      {:ex_aws_ssm, "~> 2.1"},
      {:boundary, "~> 0.10", runtime: false},
      {:code_my_spec_generators, "~> 0.1", only: :dev},
      {:wallaby, "~> 0.30", only: :test},
      {:req_cassette, "~> 0.5", only: :test}
    ]
  end

  # Aliases are shortcuts or tasks specific to the current project.
  # For example, to install project dependencies and perform other setup tasks, run:
  #
  #     $ mix setup
  #
  # See the documentation for `Mix` for more info on aliases.
  defp aliases do
    [
      setup: ["deps.get", "ecto.setup", "assets.setup", "assets.build"],
      "ecto.setup": ["ecto.create", "ecto.migrate", "run priv/repo/seeds.exs"],
      "ecto.reset": ["ecto.drop", "ecto.setup"],
      test: ["ecto.create --quiet", "ecto.migrate --quiet", "test"],
      "assets.setup": ["tailwind.install --if-missing", "esbuild.install --if-missing"],
      "assets.build": ["compile", "tailwind cleaner_crm", "esbuild cleaner_crm"],
      "assets.deploy": [
        "tailwind cleaner_crm --minify",
        "esbuild cleaner_crm --minify",
        "phx.digest"
      ],
      precommit: ["compile --warnings-as-errors", "deps.unlock --unused", "format", "test"]
    ]
  end
end

  @moduledoc """
  CleanerCrm keeps the contexts that define your domain
  and business logic.

  if it comes from the database, an external API or others.

content.text:
# provider_request

Make an arbitrary Hetzner, Cloudflare or Resend API call on the agent's
behalf, without the agent ever holding the credential.

`Hetzner`/`Cloudflare`/`Resend` each already resolve their own credential
server-side and make the authenticated call — that's the same "agent asks,
server acts" shape every other provisioning tool here already uses. This
is that plumbing, generalized: the fixed provisioning-step tools
(`run_devops_setup`, `ensure_environment`, ...) cover the sequence; this
covers everything that doesn't fit the sequence — inspecting what's
already on a shared box before adopting it, attaching a firewall to a
server that already exists, confirming something reached the provider at
all.

Reads are unrestricted. A mutating method (POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE) without
`confirm: true` is refused outright — this exists to make destructive
action against a real account deliberate, not a thing an agent can do by
constructing the wrong path on a whim. Every mutating call, confirmed or
refused, is logged with enough detail to reconstruct what happened and why.

## Arguments

  method (string, required)
  path (string, required)
  provider (string, required)
  body (object)
  confirm (boolean)
  params (object)

## Example

```lua
local result, err = provider_request({ path = "…", provider = "…", method = "…" })
if result == nil then return "failed: " .. err.message end
return result
```
